rationale: The entry's core identification — a ship as an organized kingdom, city, or state riding upon the sea of peoples — is carried directly and explicitly by its printed references. Ezekiel 27 constructs Tyre as a single vessel (boards, mast, oars, sail), then names classes of people as its parts: 'the inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men... were thy pilots' (Ezek 27:8), and closes the wreck with 'What city is like Tyrus, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea?' (Ezek 27:32) — the text itself equates the broken ship with the city. Isaiah 23 places the same maritime city among shaken kingdoms with howling ships (Isa 23:1, 11), and Revelation 18:9-19 reprises Ezekiel's lament over Babylon with the shipmasters' cry 'What city is like unto this great city!' Jonah 1 and Acts 27 fit the same frame (a vessel that can break while its people are preserved, Acts 27:22). The secondary clauses printed in the entry are also supported: rulers steering and inhabitants crewing come verbatim from Ezekiel 27:8-10; Christ ruling the waters without a vessel rests on Job 9:8 and Matthew 14:25 (walking on the sea) as quoted in the supporting chapter; and the boarded vessel coming under its true Head rests on Mark 4:36-41, where the ship carries Him but His word, not the ship, commands wind and sea. The strongest counter — ship as the Church — cannot explain the printed references at all: Tyre and Babylon are condemned commercial polities, not the Church. Moreover, the Church reading is a narrower special case that the entry's second clause explicitly accommodates (a governed company under Christ its Head), so it does not contradict the core referent. The book's definition unifies Ezekiel, Isaiah, Revelation, Jonah, Acts, and the Gospel boat scenes under one mechanism; the Church reading must fragment them into unrelated context-dependent uses.
book_core_identification: A ship symbolizes an organized political body — a kingdom, city, or state — riding upon the sea, where the sea is the mass of peoples; the vessel is the bounded governed structure carried by and standing over that population.
book_secondary_elaborations: Its rulers (pilots) steer it and its inhabitants crew it (Ezek 27:8-10).
Christ can rule the waters directly without any vessel (Job 9:8; Matt 14:25), unlike earthly rulers who need a constructed ship to stand above the peoples.
When Christ boards a ship, the vessel and its company come under their true Head; the ship carries Him but does not confer authority on Him (Mark 4:36-41).
chapter_only_objections: The identification of Jerusalem/Judea as the ship in John 11:48-50, with Caiaphas's bargain paralleling Jonah's crew surrendering one man, is an interpretive typology not asserted in the entry.
The reading of Peter's sinking (Matt 14:29-30) as fear of the people/tumult displacing trust is a devotional application beyond the printed definition.
The claim that Mark 4:1 stages Jesus 'sitting in the sea' as an enthronement echoing Psalm 29:10 is suggestive but not demonstrated.
The deferred claim that Acts 27–28 is a 'lived similitude' whose complete meaning 'requires a study of its own' is an unargued promissory note.
The assertion that 'the beasts later stand openly for peoples and kingdoms' in the Noah discussion imports a separate symbol not established here.
Reliance on Greco-Roman ship-of-state parallels (Alcaeus, Aeschylus, Plato, Horace) is extra-biblical corroboration of recognition, not derivation.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The ship primarily symbolizes the Church — the vessel of salvation carrying believers safely through the sea of the world toward eternal life, rooted in patristic tradition (Tertullian, Hippolytus, Cyprian), the Gospel storm narratives, Peter's boat (the 'barque of Peter'), and the typology of Noah's ark with 1 Peter 3:20-21.
counter_core_identification: Ship = the Church, the divinely preserved community of salvation navigating the hostile world under Christ's protection.
material_core_denial: There is no material denial of the book's core. The Church-as-ship reading identifies one specific governed company under Christ its Head — precisely the case the entry's second clause describes ('when He boards one it comes under its true Head'). It is a narrower instance, not a rival referent, and it offers no account of Tyre or Babylon as ships that would exclude the polity reading.
counter_case: Patristic and liturgical tradition (nave, barque of Peter, WCC logo) treats the ship as the Church, giving the reading enormous historical weight.

The Gospel boat narratives (Matt 8:23-27; Mark 4:35-41; Luke 5:1-11) are naturally read as the Church buffeted but safe with Christ aboard, and Hilary of Poitiers already read the ship as a type of the Church.
1 Peter 3:20-21 explicitly links Noah's ark to baptism and salvation, anchoring the vessel-of-salvation typology in the New Testament itself.
book_explanatory_advantages: Ezekiel 27 is the one passage where Scripture itself decodes the symbol: it builds the ship, mans it with named classes of a polity, and calls the wreck a city (27:32) — direct textual definition rather than post-biblical tradition.

The definition unifies the negative ship texts (Tyre, Babylon, Jonah's vessel, the ships of Tarshish) and the positive ones (the disciples' boat under Christ) under one mechanism, whereas the Church reading must treat the negative texts as an unrelated separate symbol.

It explains the cross-text machinery: Revelation 18 deliberately reprises Ezekiel 27's lament over a city; Isaiah 23:11 pairs howling ships with shaken kingdoms; Acts 27:22 shows the vessel perishing while its people survive — the organized body and its members distinguished.
It coheres with the sea-as-peoples symbol (explicit in Rev 17:15's tradition and the book's system), giving the ship a defined position: government riding upon the population.
It explains why Christ walks on the sea (Job 9:8) while earthly powers must build ships — a contrast the Church reading does not address.
It handles the ark honestly, noting the Hebrew tevah is not the ordinary ship word, so the ark/baptism typology does not fix the meaning of 'ship'.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Overwhelming weight of interpretive tradition from the second century onward.
Natural devotional fit with the Gospel storm scenes and Peter's boat.
Direct New Testament warrant for the ark-salvation typology (1 Pet 3:20-21), though for the ark rather than the ordinary ship.
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 27:3-9 (city constructed as a ship; inhabitants as mariners, wise men as pilots)
Ezekiel 27:26-32 ('the east wind hath broken thee... What city is like Tyrus, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea?')
Isaiah 23:1, 11 (ships of Tarshish howl; the LORD 'shook the kingdoms')
Revelation 18:9-19 (Babylon's fall sung in Ezekiel's ship-lament by shipmasters: 'What city is like unto this great city!')
Acts 27:22 (loss of the ship but no loss of life — the organized body distinguished from its people)
Mark 4:36-41 and Matthew 14:25 with Job 9:8 (Christ commands the sea from the ship and walks upon it without one)
unresolved_objections: The entry's definition is a synthesis; no single verse states 'a ship is a kingdom, city, or state,' though Ezekiel 27:32 comes very close by naming the wrecked vessel a city.

The heavy weight of the Church-as-ship tradition means the entry departs from the historically dominant gloss, though the entry's Christ-as-true-Head clause substantially absorbs that tradition as a special case.
